title: The Undershepherd
subtitle: Pastoral Leadership, Authority, and the Care of God's People
blurb: The pastor is not the shepherd. He is an under-shepherd, holding a borrowed staff over a flock that was never his, answerable to the One whose blood bought them. This book refuses the two cheap roads — domination and abandonment — and argues that the only authority worth having in the church is the kind that bleeds for the sheep instead of feeding on them.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Staff
chapters.summary: The shepherd metaphor is not decoration. It is a claim about ownership, and every pastoral failure begins the moment a man forgets the flock is not his.
chapters.body:
The first lie a pastor believes is small. It is not pride in the obvious sense, not the lust for a bigger platform or a louder name. It is quieter than that. It is the slow, almost invisible substitution of a possessive pronoun. My church. My people. My ministry. The grammar shifts before the heart does, and by the time a man notices, the theology has already rotted underneath the words.

The shepherd image runs the length of Scripture, and it is never flattering to the shepherd. When Ezekiel turns to the leaders of Israel, he does not begin with their technique. He begins with ownership. "Woe to the shepherds of Israel who have been feeding themselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep?" (Ezekiel 34:2). The indictment is not incompetence. It is theft. They treated a flock that belonged to God as though it belonged to them, and a flock you think you own is a flock you will eventually eat.

Peter knew this, and Peter had reason to know it. The man who wrote "shepherd the flock of God that is among you" (1 Peter 5:2) had once been told three times, over a fire, after a betrayal, to feed sheep that were not his own (John 21:17). He did not arrive at the metaphor through study. He arrived at it through failure. The charge to feed the lambs came to a man who had just learned, in the most public way available to him, that he was not the rock he thought he was. That is the soil pastoral authority grows in. Not strength. Repentance.

Here is the distinction that governs everything else in this book. There is one Shepherd. "The Lord is my shepherd," David writes, and the whole of Psalm 23 is built on a possessive that belongs to God alone — the sheep are His, the green pastures are His, the rod and the staff that comfort are held in His hand (Psalm 23:1). When Jesus stands up in John 10 and says "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11), He is closing a door that men have been trying to walk through for centuries. The definite article is His. The good shepherd is not a category pastors enter. It is a Person we serve under.

This is why Peter, when he gives the elders their charge, immediately points them upward. "And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory" (1 Peter 5:4). The word matters. Chief Shepherd. Which makes every other shepherd a subordinate, a deputy, a man holding a staff he did not carve over sheep he did not buy. The Latin tradition gave us the title that the Reformed churches kept: the pastor is the *minister*, the servant, and the older shepherds knew it. Gregory the Great, dragged toward the office he did not want, wrote his *Pastoral Rule* around exactly this fear — that the man given charge of souls would forget he was a steward and begin to behave like an owner.

I have felt the pull. I will not pretend I have not. There are Sunday mornings when a man looks out over a room he has labored in for years and feels something rise that is not gratitude. It is proprietorship. These are the people I gathered. This is the building I filled. This is the ministry I built. And every one of those sentences is a small theft, because not one of those things is true. I gathered no one the Spirit did not draw. I filled no room the Father did not call. I built nothing the Son did not buy with His own blood, and the blood is the whole argument. Paul says it to the Ephesian elders without softening it: care for "the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood" (Acts 20:28). You did not pay for them. He did.

So the staff is borrowed. Sit with that, because it changes the weight of the whole vocation. A man caring for his own property may do as he likes with it. A man caring for another's property is accountable to its owner, and the accounting is the thing most pastors never want to think about until it is too late. Eugene Peterson spent decades insisting that pastoral work had been quietly converted into something else — management, performance, the running of a religious shop — and what had been lost in the conversion was precisely this sense of holding something that is not yours, before Someone who will ask for it back.

The borrowed staff is not a diminishment. This is the part the anxious pastor misses. To hold authority you did not generate, over people you did not purchase, on behalf of a Shepherd who actually loves them more than you do — that is not a smaller calling. It is a safer one. The man who believes the flock is his carries a weight that will crush him, because he is trying to be a savior to people who already have one. The man who knows the flock is Christ's can finally exhale. He is not the rescuer. He is the under-shepherd who points to the rescuer. He can fail and the sheep will still be kept, because they were never being kept by him.

There is freedom in the borrowed staff, and there is terror in it, and the two arrive together. The freedom is that you are not the Christ. The terror is that you will answer to Him. Both are true. Both are mercy. The man who feels only the freedom becomes careless. The man who feels only the terror becomes a tyrant or a coward. The shepherd who holds both — light enough to rest, sober enough to tremble — is the one beginning to understand what he has been handed.

Calvin, commenting on the pastoral office, kept returning to the idea that ministers are instruments, that God could feed His people directly and chooses instead to use men, and that this is condescension on God's part rather than promotion on ours. We are the means He stoops to use. Not the source. Never the source.

So begin here. Before the questions of authority and discipline and the hireling and the long accounting, begin with the pronoun. Whose are they? If your answer comes too quickly, you have not understood the question. The sheep are not yours. The staff is not yours. The pasture is not yours.

You are holding something that belongs to Someone else. He is watching how you hold it. And one day, He is going to ask for it back.
chapters.verdict: You hold a staff you did not carve, over sheep you did not buy.
reflect: Whose flock do you actually believe you are leading?
Where have you started speaking of "my people" as if they were property?
What would change tomorrow if you genuinely held the staff as borrowed?

chapters.title: Authority That Bleeds
chapters.summary: Real pastoral authority exists, but it is exercised through self-spending love, not dominance — the cross is the model and the limit.
chapters.body:
The church has a habit of overcorrecting, and the overcorrection on authority is as dangerous as the abuse it answers. A generation watched pastors wield power like petty kings, and the reaction was to declare that pastoral authority is itself the problem — that any man who claims to lead a flock is already halfway to abuse. This is sentimental, and it is unbiblical, and it leaves the sheep worse off than it found them. Sheep without a shepherd are not free. They are scattered.

Jesus did not abolish authority. He redefined its center of gravity. When the disciples argued about greatness — and they argued about it constantly, which should comfort every pastor who has ever wanted the bigger chair — He did not tell them to stop wanting to lead. He told them what leading costs. "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant" (Matthew 20:25-26). Notice He does not say there will be no great ones. He says greatness will be inverted. The throne is real. It is just shaped like a basin and a towel.

This is the thing the church on both ends keeps getting wrong. The authoritarian hears "authority is real" and stops listening. The egalitarian hears "it shall not be so among you" and stops listening. But the sentence is one sentence. Authority is real, and it is exercised downward, through service, at cost. Remove either half and you have built something Jesus did not.

Peter, again, says it plainly to the elders: shepherd the flock "not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). The Greek behind "domineering" is the language of lording over, of pressing down with the weight of office. Peter forbids it. And then in the same breath he assumes the elders have real charge, real responsibility, a real flock allotted to them. He does not resolve the tension by deleting the authority. He resolves it by changing how it moves. Down, not over. Through example, not through pressure.

What does authority that bleeds actually look like on a Tuesday? It looks like a man who has the institutional power to win an argument and chooses to absorb the cost instead. It looks like a pastor who could enforce his preference and instead lays it down, not because he lacks the standing to insist but because he has learned where insisting leads. The world's authority spends other people to protect itself. Christ's authority spends itself to protect other people. That is the entire difference, and it is visible in five minutes of any elders' meeting.

Bonhoeffer understood the temptation precisely. In his work on Christian community he warned against the leader who makes himself indispensable, who builds the flock's dependence on his own person rather than on Christ, who confuses the strength of his personality with the work of the Spirit. The man who needs to be needed will quietly arrange a congregation around his own wounds. He will call it shepherding. It is feeding. And the line between the two is not the amount of work done — both men work hard — but the direction the spending flows. Toward the sheep, or toward the self.

I have caught myself on the wrong side of that line, and I will name it because the whole structure of this book depends on the man writing it standing inside the indictment. There have been seasons when I confused my own need for affirmation with the congregation's need for leadership. When I held a position not because it was right but because retreating would have wounded my standing. When the authority I exercised was protecting me, not them. That is not pastoral authority. That is the thing Peter forbade, dressed in pastoral language. I did this. Not a category of pastors out there. Me.

The cross is both the model and the limit. The model, because it shows what authority looks like when it is healthy — total, costly, self-giving, aimed entirely at the good of the other. "The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11). That is the picture. But it is also the limit, because the cross sets a boundary no pastor may cross: he may never make the sheep bleed for him. The direction is fixed. The shepherd bleeds for the flock. The flock does not exist to bleed for the shepherd. Every abuse in the history of the church is some version of reversing that arrow.

Augustine, preaching to his own congregation on the shepherds of Ezekiel 34, made the distinction sharp. He told them that he was, with them, a sheep under the one Shepherd, and that he was, for them, set in a place of care — and that the danger of his office was precisely the danger of feeding himself with the milk and clothing himself with the wool while neglecting the weak and the sick and the lost. He preached against his own temptation in front of the people who could see whether he was living it. That is authority that bleeds. It exposes itself to the very flock it leads.

Keller used to frame leadership through the logic of the gospel itself — that the Christian leader, having received everything as grace, has nothing left to defend, and is therefore free to lead without the desperate self-protection that marks worldly power. The man who knows he is justified does not need the office to justify him. He can hold authority loosely because his identity is not riding on it. The man whose identity is riding on the office will grip it until his knuckles are white, and a white-knuckled grip on a flock always leaves bruises.

So we are left with a kind of authority the world cannot recognize, because the world measures authority by what it can make others do, and this kind is measured by what it is willing to suffer. It does not abdicate. It does not dominate. It bleeds.

Find a pastor with real authority in a congregation and trace it back to its source. It will not be his eloquence, though he may be eloquent. It will not be his strategy, though he may be wise. It will be the accumulated evidence, gathered over years, that this man has consistently spent himself for these people and asked nothing back. That is authority no committee can grant and no scandal can fully erase. It is bought the only way it has ever been bought.

With blood. His own.
chapters.verdict: The only authority Christ honors is the kind willing to die.
reflect: Do you secure your authority by serving or by controlling?
When was the last time your leadership cost you something the congregation never saw?
Whose pattern of authority are you actually imitating — Christ's or the world's?

chapters.title: The Hireling
chapters.summary: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who owns the sheep with the hireling who works for wages and flees when the cost rises — and the hireling is rarely obvious from the outside.
chapters.body:
There is a figure in John 10 that every pastor should be afraid of becoming, and almost none of us think we are. Jesus introduces him without ceremony. "He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them. He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep" (John 10:12-13). The hireling. The wage-worker. The man who does the job of shepherding without the heart of a shepherd.

What makes the hireling terrifying is that on an ordinary day, he is indistinguishable from the real thing. He feeds the sheep. He leads them to water. He stands in the field looking exactly like a shepherd, because in calm weather the difference does not show. The hireling and the shepherd both work. They use the same staff, walk the same fields, speak the same words. The distinction is invisible until the wolf arrives, and then the difference is total. One man runs. One man stays. The wolf does not create the difference. The wolf reveals what was already there.

This means the hireling is mostly hidden from the congregation, and worse, often hidden from himself. A man can pastor for twenty years and never know which one he is, because the wolf has not come yet. He has had a comfortable tenure, a stable salary, a congregation that mostly liked him, and the test that would have exposed his heart never showed up. He thinks his calm field is evidence of his faithfulness. It is only evidence that the wolf has not come.

The hireling's defining trait is not laziness and not cruelty. It is the structure of his motivation. He serves for the wages. The wages may be money — let us not be naive about that, the love of money has hollowed out plenty of pulpits — but the wages are more often subtler. The wage of approval. The wage of being needed. The wage of a comfortable life, a respected name in the community, a calendar full of meaningful work. None of these are evil in themselves. They become the hireling's wages when they are the reason the man stays. And the moment staying costs more than the wages are worth, he is gone — physically, or worse, internally, while his body remains in the pulpit.

I have watched this happen, and I have felt its gravity in my own chest, so I will not write about the hireling as though he lives only in other men. There are weeks when I notice my own motivation drifting toward the wage. When I find myself measuring a sermon by how it landed rather than by whether it was true. When I catch myself avoiding the hard conversation not because it would harm the sheep but because it would cost me their warmth. That drift toward the wage is the hireling's pull, and no pastor is exempt from it. The question is not whether you feel it. The question is what you do when you feel it.

The contrast Jesus draws is ownership. "I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me... and I lay down my life for the sheep" (John 10:14-15). The shepherd stays because the sheep are his. The hireling flees because they are not. Now here is the difficulty for the under-shepherd, because we established in the first chapter that the sheep are not yours — they belong to Christ. So how does a man who does not own the sheep avoid becoming the hireling who does not own the sheep?

The answer is the difference between legal ownership and given love. The under-shepherd does not own the flock, but he is not a wage-worker either, because the Chief Shepherd has given him the sheep to love as his own. Paul calls Timothy his true child, the Thessalonians his glory and joy, the Galatians his little children for whom he is again in the anguish of childbirth (Galatians 4:19). That is not the language of a hired hand. That is a man who has received a flock as a gift and bound his own heart to it as if it were his blood. He has no legal title. He has something stronger. He has love that has accepted the cost in advance.

Richard Baxter, in his *Reformed Pastor*, pressed this on the ministers of his day with an intensity that still stings to read. He charged them to know their people individually, to labor over each soul as a man labors over his own children, to refuse the kind of distant, professional ministry that handles souls in the aggregate. Baxter understood that the hireling can love a crowd. Only the shepherd loves the sheep one at a time, by name, at cost. The hireling preaches to the room. The shepherd knows who is missing from it.

The wolf, in our settings, rarely has fangs you can see. It is the scandal that splits a congregation and asks the pastor whether he will stay and bleed through the repair or quietly send out his résumé. It is the long illness of a difficult member who needs years of unrewarding care. It is the season when the church declines and the wages thin out and staying means accepting a diminished name. It is the moment when telling the truth will cost the pastor the affection he has been living on. Every one of these is a wolf, and every one of them asks the same question the wolf in John 10 asks. Will you flee, or will you stay?

Eugene Peterson spent a career warning that the pastoral vocation had been professionalized into a career, and the professionalization is exactly the soil the hireling grows in. A career is a thing you advance. A vocation is a thing you answer. The man who treats the pastorate as a career will move when the career calls for it, and he will tell himself it was the Lord's leading, and sometimes it will have been, and sometimes it will have been the hireling fleeing the wolf with a spiritual vocabulary to cover his tracks.

So examine the wages. Not whether you receive them — every laborer is worth his hire, and Scripture defends the pastor's pay (1 Timothy 5:17-18). The question is whether the wages are the reason. Strip away the approval, the security, the comfortable name. If those were gone tomorrow and the wolf were at the gate, would you stay?

You will not know the true answer until the wolf comes. But you can know which way your heart is leaning while the field is still calm. The hireling leans toward the wages. The shepherd leans toward the sheep.

Lean, while there is still time to feel which way you fall.
chapters.verdict: The wolf does not reveal the hireling. The wolf only confirms him.
reflect: At what cost would you leave this flock, and is that price quietly negotiable?
Where do you serve for the wages — approval, security, comfort — rather than for the sheep?
What does the congregation see that the wolf has not yet tested?

chapters.title: Against the Shepherds of Israel
chapters.summary: Ezekiel 34 is the clearest indictment of pastoral abuse in Scripture, and its specifics — neglect, exploitation, harshness — map precisely onto modern ministry failure.
chapters.body:
The most frightening chapter in the Bible for a pastor is not in the New Testament. It is Ezekiel 34, and it should be read slowly, in the first person, by anyone who stands behind a pulpit. God does not generalize. He itemizes. And the items are specific enough that no shepherd can hide behind the vagueness of his own self-assessment.

"Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep" (Ezekiel 34:2-3). The first charge is consumption. The shepherds had reversed the flow. The flock existed to sustain them rather than the other way around. They took the fat and the wool and the meat — the produce of the sheep, the things the sheep were supposed to receive care in exchange for — and they kept it for themselves. The relationship had become parasitic. The pastor was feeding on the very people he was called to feed.

Then comes the second charge, and it is the one that indicts most of us, because it is a sin of omission rather than commission. "The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought" (Ezekiel 34:4). Read that list again. It is not a list of things the shepherds did. It is a list of things they failed to do. They did not have to abuse anyone to earn God's woe. They only had to neglect. The weak went unstrengthened. The sick went unhealed. The strayed went unsought. And for this — for absence, for inattention, for the soft sin of not bothering — God rises in judgment.

I find this more searching than the charge of exploitation, because almost no pastor sets out to consume his flock, but nearly every pastor is tempted to neglect the difficult ones. The weak member who drains energy. The sick saint whose visits never seem productive. The strayed family who left in anger and would have to be pursued at the cost of pride. The lost soul on the edge of the congregation who never quite belonged. These are the four categories Ezekiel names, and they are precisely the four categories a busy pastor learns to let slip. We attend to the strong because the strong reinforce us. We let the weak and the sick and the strayed and the lost fall off the edge of the calendar, and we call it priorities, and God calls it the abandonment of the flock.

Then the third charge: "with force and harshness you have ruled them" (Ezekiel 34:4). Here is the authoritarian sin, the lording-over that Peter would later forbid. When the shepherds did engage the sheep, they engaged them with force. They used the staff to beat rather than to guide. This is the pastor who controls through fear, who governs by guilt, who keeps the flock in line through intimidation dressed as conviction. He is not absent like the neglectful shepherd. He is present in the worst possible way — present as a threat rather than a comfort.

The consequence God names is devastating in its logic. "So they were scattered, because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the wild beasts" (Ezekiel 34:5). The failure of the shepherds did not stay contained to the shepherds. It scattered the sheep. The flock dispersed and became prey. This is the thing pastors rarely reckon with — that pastoral failure is never a private matter. When the shepherd fails, the sheep are scattered, and scattered sheep are eaten. The wolves do not need to break in. The shepherd's negligence opens the gate for them.

I have been the harsh shepherd in small ways I did not see at the time, and I have been the neglectful one in ways I saw and excused. I have let the difficult member fall off the calendar because the calendar was full of things that affirmed me more. I have ruled, in moments, with more force than care, and called it leadership. The reason Ezekiel 34 is the most frightening chapter for me is that I cannot read its list without finding myself somewhere on it. We did this. I did this. The shepherds of Israel are not a historical curiosity. They are a mirror.

But the chapter does not end in indictment, and the turn is the whole gospel of pastoral ministry. God says: "Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out... I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep" (Ezekiel 34:11, 15). When the human shepherds fail, God does not abandon the flock. He removes the false shepherds and takes up the staff Himself. "I will rescue my flock; they shall no longer be a prey" (Ezekiel 34:22). And then the prophecy reaches forward to a single shepherd who will do what the many failed to do: "I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall feed them" (Ezekiel 34:23).

That one Shepherd is Christ. The whole indictment of the false shepherds resolves into the promise of the true one. Which means Ezekiel 34 is not only a warning to pastors. It is a gospel for the scattered sheep, and it is the standard against which every under-shepherd is measured. Christ does what Ezekiel describes. He seeks the lost. He brings back the strayed. He binds up the injured. He strengthens the weak. And He says, in language that echoes the prophet directly, "I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also" (John 10:16). The Good Shepherd of John 10 is the fulfillment of the promised Shepherd of Ezekiel 34. He is what the false shepherds were not.

So the question for the under-shepherd is brutally simple. Are you imitating the shepherds God removed, or the Shepherd God sent? The test is in the four categories. Find the weak in your flock and ask whether you have strengthened them. Find the sick and ask whether you have gone to them. Find the strayed and ask whether you have pursued them. Find the lost and ask whether you have sought them. If the honest answer to those four is no, then you are standing in Ezekiel 34, and you are not standing among the shepherds God praised.

There is still time to put down the force and take up the search. There is still time to leave the ninety-nine and go after the one. But there is not infinite time, because the chapter is clear about what God does when the shepherds will not.

He takes the flock back. And He feeds it Himself.
chapters.verdict: God does not merely correct bad shepherds. He removes them and feeds the flock Himself.
reflect: Which of Ezekiel's specific charges fits you most closely right now?
Who in your flock is weak, sick, or straying — and have you gone after them?
Are you ruling the sheep with force, or seeking them with care?

chapters.title: Feed My Sheep
chapters.summary: The restoration of Peter in John 21 ties the entire pastoral vocation to a single command repeated three times — and grounds it in love for Christ before love for the flock.
chapters.body:
The most important conversation about pastoral ministry in the Gospels does not happen in a seminary or a synagogue. It happens on a beach, over breakfast, between a risen Lord and a man who had failed Him completely. John 21 is where the pastoral vocation is forged, and it is forged in the fire of restoration, which is the only fire hot enough to make a shepherd.

Peter had denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (John 18:18). Now, in John 21, there is another charcoal fire — the same word, deliberately chosen — and beside it Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves Him. The geography is intentional. The number is intentional. Jesus is not rubbing Peter's nose in the failure. He is healing it at the exact site where it occurred. Three denials, three questions, three commissions. The wound is being closed stitch by stitch, in the same place it was opened.

And here is what should arrest every pastor: the commission is attached to the love, not the other way around. Jesus does not ask Peter about his competence. He does not ask about his leadership philosophy, his strategic vision, his ability to grow a movement. He asks one question, three times. "Simon, son of John, do you love me?" (John 21:16). And only after the answer comes does the charge follow. "Feed my lambs." "Tend my sheep." "Feed my sheep" (John 21:15-17). The whole pastoral office hangs on the love. No love for Christ, no feeding of His sheep. The order cannot be reversed.

This is the thing that gets lost in every conversation about ministry skill. We assess pastors by their gifting, their charisma, their ability to fill a room. Jesus assesses Peter by a single question that has nothing to do with any of that. Do you love me? Because the man who loves Christ will care for what Christ loves, and the man who does not love Christ will eventually care for himself, however gifted he is. The feeding flows from the loving. Drain the loving and the feeding becomes performance — a man going through the motions of care because it is his job, which is to say, the hireling.

Notice also that the sheep are emphatically Christ's. My lambs. My sheep. My sheep. Three times the possessive belongs to Jesus. We are back to the borrowed staff. Peter is not given a flock to own. He is given Christ's flock to feed. The commission to shepherd is simultaneously a reminder that the shepherd is not the owner. Even in the act of handing Peter the staff, Jesus keeps title to the sheep.

But fix your attention on the verb. Feed. Tend. Feed. The pastoral task, reduced to its essence, is feeding. Not entertaining. Not managing. Not building. Feeding. The sheep need to eat, and what they eat is the Word of God, and the shepherd's primary labor is to set that food before them. This is why Paul tells Timothy to "preach the word" and to do it "in season and out of season" (2 Timothy 4:2), and why he warns that a time is coming when people "will not endure sound teaching" but will accumulate teachers to suit their own appetites (2 Timothy 4:3). The hungry sheep want to be fed; the itching ear wants to be tickled. The shepherd's job is to feed even when the flock would rather be tickled.

Eugene Peterson built much of his work on the conviction that pastors had abandoned this feeding for something busier and more impressive. He described the temptation to become a religious entrepreneur, running programs and managing an organization, while the actual work of feeding souls on Scripture and prayer quietly disappeared. The pastor was everywhere except in the one place his vocation required — present with the Word, present with the sheep, doing the slow unglamorous work of feeding. Peterson called it, in essence, the difference between a job that looks like ministry and the vocation that actually is ministry. The activity can be enormous while the feeding is nonexistent.

I know this temptation intimately, because the feeding is hard and the managing is flattering. It is more satisfying to launch a program than to sit with the Word until it has something to give the sheep. It is more affirming to grow an organization than to feed a soul who will never thank you. I have spent weeks doing the work that looks like ministry and realized I had not actually fed anyone — I had administered, I had performed, I had managed, but the sheep went home hungry because the shepherd had not eaten first. I did this. I confess it because the chapter demands the confession.

Now return to the question, because the question is also for us. Jesus does not ask Peter, "Are you skilled enough to lead my church?" He asks, "Do you love me?" And every pastor must let that question land before he is fit to feed anyone. The ministry that is not the answer to that question is a ministry built on the wrong foundation. The conferences, the strategies, the leadership books — none of them ask the question Jesus asked. They ask whether you can lead. He asks whether you love Him. And the second question is the only one that produces a shepherd rather than a manager.

There is a tenderness here that the rest of this book's prophetic edge should not obscure. Jesus restores Peter before He commissions him. The failure does not disqualify the man; the restoration requalifies him. Peter will go on to write to elders about shepherding the flock of God precisely because he is a man who failed and was restored, and so he knows that the shepherd is first a forgiven sheep. The order matters here too. Restoration first. Commission second. A man who tries to feed sheep without first being restored by Christ will feed them out of his own emptiness, and an empty shepherd starves the flock while pretending to serve it.

So the chapter leaves the under-shepherd with two things to hold. The first is the command, clear and unrepeatable: feed the sheep. Not entertain them, not manage them, not build something impressive on top of them. Feed them the Word until they are no longer hungry. The second is the condition, prior to the command and underneath it: do you love Me? Because the feeding is only real if the love is real, and the love is only real if it has faced the risen Christ across the fire where the failure happened and answered the question honestly.

Peter answered it three times, and the third time he was grieved, and his grief was the proof that the answer was true. "Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you" (John 21:17). That grief is where shepherding begins. Not in confidence. In the broken, restored, tearful certainty that you love the One whose sheep you are about to feed.

Answer the question first. Then, and only then, pick up the staff.
chapters.verdict: You cannot feed sheep you do not love for a Shepherd you have not faced.
reflect: Has your love for Christ been restored after your failures, or merely buried?
Are you feeding the sheep, or entertaining them, or managing them?
What in your ministry is the answer to a question Jesus has actually asked you?

chapters.title: The Long Walk Through the Valley
chapters.summary: Psalm 23 is a map of how the Shepherd leads — through abundance and through death — and the under-shepherd must learn to lead the same way, into hard places rather than around them.
chapters.body:
Psalm 23 has been domesticated. We have hung it on funeral home walls and embroidered it on pillows until it sounds like a sedative. It is not a sedative. It is a battle hymn about being led through the territory of death by a Shepherd who refuses to go around it. And it teaches the under-shepherd something the comfortable pastor never learns: that real shepherding means leading the flock through the valley, not merely beside the waters.

The psalm opens in abundance, and we love this part. "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters" (Psalm 23:1-2). Green pastures. Still waters. Rest and provision and the deep exhale of a sheep that lacks nothing. This is the shepherd's work at its most pleasant — leading the flock to abundance, watching them rest, providing what they need. And many pastors are good at this part. They can lead a congregation through a season of growth and blessing. The waters are still and they look like competent shepherds.

But the psalm does not stay in the pasture. "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me" (Psalm 23:4). The Shepherd leads the sheep into the valley. He does not lead them around it. He does not abandon them at its edge. He takes them through it — through the dark ravine, the narrow place where predators hide and the path drops into shadow. And the comfort of the psalm is not that the Shepherd keeps the sheep out of the valley. It is that He is with them in it. "For you are with me." The presence, not the absence of danger, is the comfort.

This is the part of shepherding that separates the under-shepherds. Anyone can lead beside still waters. The test is whether a man will lead his flock through the valley — into the hard sermon series, the painful church discipline, the financial sacrifice, the confrontation of a beloved sin, the season of decline that faithfulness sometimes requires. The shepherd who only ever leads toward comfort is not actually leading. He is following the flock's preferences and calling it leadership. The Shepherd of Psalm 23 leads into the valley because the valley is where the flock has to go, and a shepherd who will only go where it is pleasant is no shepherd at all.

I have stood at the mouth of valleys and chosen the path around them. I have softened a sermon because the truth in it would have led the congregation into a hard place I did not want the cost of leading them through. I have avoided the confrontation, smoothed over the conflict, kept the waters artificially still because still waters are easier to manage than a valley walk. And every time, I was choosing my own comfort over the flock's need to be led through to the other side. The sheep did not need to be kept beside the waters forever. They needed to be led through the valley to the table that waits beyond it. I kept them in the meadow because the meadow was easier for me. I did this.

Notice what comforts the sheep in the valley: "your rod and your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). The rod and the staff are instruments of authority — the rod to fight off predators, the staff to guide and rescue the straying sheep. And in the valley, these instruments of authority are experienced as comfort. This is the answer to everything we said about authority earlier. When authority is exercised by a shepherd who is leading the flock through danger for their own good, the flock does not experience that authority as a threat. They experience it as comfort. The rod that beats the wolf and the staff that hooks the falling sheep are not weapons against the flock. They are the flock's security in the dark.

The reason so many congregations have come to fear pastoral authority is that they have only experienced the rod and staff turned against them, never deployed on their behalf. They have known the shepherd's force, as Ezekiel said, but not the shepherd's protection. And so they have concluded that authority itself is the enemy. But Psalm 23 corrects this. In the hand of a shepherd who is leading you through the valley of death because he loves you, the rod and the staff are the most comforting things in the world. The problem was never the authority. The problem was the direction it pointed.

Then the table: "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). The destination of the valley walk is a feast. The Shepherd does not lead the sheep into the valley to lose them there. He leads them through it to a table set on the other side, in full view of the enemies who could not stop the journey. This is the hope that sustains the shepherd's willingness to lead through hard places. The valley is not the end. The table is. And a pastor who has internalized this can lead his flock into the necessary darkness without despair, because he knows what waits beyond it. He is not leading them into death. He is leading them through the shadow of death to a feast that death cannot crash.

The psalm ends not with the sheep pursuing comfort but with comfort pursuing the sheep. "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord forever" (Psalm 23:6). The word translated "follow" is closer to "pursue" — goodness and mercy chase the sheep down all the days of life. The Shepherd's care is not passive. It hunts the sheep across the whole of their existence and runs them home. And the under-shepherd's task is to be, in his small and borrowed way, an instrument of that pursuit — a man through whom the Chief Shepherd's goodness and mercy chase down the sheep and bring them home.

Brueggemann taught that the psalms of trust like this one are not naive — they are spoken by people who know exactly how dark the valley is and choose trust anyway, in defiance of the darkness, as an act of faith rather than an absence of knowledge. Psalm 23 is not written by someone who has never seen death. It is written by someone who walks through its shadow and refuses to let the shadow have the last word, because the Shepherd is present in it. That is the courage the under-shepherd must learn. Not the avoidance of the valley, but the willingness to walk into it with the flock, trusting the One who walks ahead.

So lead them through. The waters are good, and there is a time for the meadow, and the flock needs the rest the green pastures give. But do not mistake the meadow for the whole of shepherding. The Shepherd you serve under leads His sheep through the valley of the shadow of death, and He expects His under-shepherds to do the same — to go ahead into the dark place, rod and staff in hand, and bring the flock through to the table on the other side.

The shepherd who will only walk in the sunlight has not yet learned the trade.
chapters.verdict: A shepherd who only leads beside still waters has never truly led at all.
reflect: Where are you avoiding leading your flock through a valley because it would cost you?
Do the sheep experience your presence most when the going is hardest?
What does it mean that the rod and staff comfort rather than threaten?

chapters.title: Discipline as the Severe Mercy
chapters.summary: Church discipline, rightly understood, is not punishment but the most demanding form of pastoral care — the pursuit of the straying sheep — and its absence is a failure of love.
chapters.body:
The word "discipline" has been poisoned, and the poison has cost the church dearly. We hear it and think punishment, exclusion, the cold machinery of religious power crushing a sinner. And so the church has largely abandoned it, congratulating itself on its grace while the sheep wander off cliffs unpursued. But church discipline, in Scripture, is not the opposite of care. It is one of its most demanding forms. It is the pursuit of the straying sheep, and a shepherd who will not pursue is not gracious. He is negligent.

Return to Ezekiel's list for a moment: "the strayed you have not brought back" (Ezekiel 34:4). The failure to pursue the wandering sheep is named there as a charge against the false shepherds. The good shepherd, by contrast, "leaves the ninety-nine on the mountains and goes in search of the one that went astray" (Matthew 18:12). And it is no accident that this parable of the pursued sheep sits in Matthew 18 immediately before the most direct passage on church discipline in the Gospels. Jesus connects them on purpose. The seeking of the lost sheep and the confronting of the sinning brother are the same impulse. Both are pursuit. Both are love that refuses to let the straying stray unchallenged.

"If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone" (Matthew 18:15). The whole procedure that follows — the private conversation, then the two or three witnesses, then the church — is escalation, but it is escalation in the service of recovery. The goal is stated at the start: "If he listens to you, you have gained your brother." Gained. The point of every step is to gain the brother back. Even the final step, treating the unrepentant one "as a Gentile and a tax collector" (Matthew 18:17), must be read remembering how Jesus treated Gentiles and tax collectors — He pursued them, ate with them, called them. The "excommunication" is not abandonment. It is a change in the form of pursuit, an attempt to let the sinner feel the reality of his separation so that he might come home.

This is the part the avoidant pastor will not accept: that refusing to discipline is itself a failure to love. We tell ourselves that not confronting the straying sheep is gracious, that we are extending mercy, that we are being like Jesus. But Jesus pursued. He confronted. He named sin specifically and called for repentance directly. The pastor who watches a member destroy his marriage, or harm the flock, or wander into sin, and says nothing because confrontation feels unkind, is not being like Jesus. He is being like the hireling who sees the wolf and does nothing. The wolf, in this case, is the sin itself, and the shepherd who will not confront it is letting it devour the sheep.

A church that will not discipline does not love its people. It only likes them. Liking people means wanting them to be comfortable, untroubled, pleased with you. Loving people means wanting their good even at the cost of their comfort and your standing. The pastor who likes his flock will never confront them, because confrontation risks the warmth he lives on. The pastor who loves his flock will confront when confrontation is what the sheep needs, because he wants the sheep restored more than he wants to be liked. And these two pastors can look identical for years, right up until the moment the straying begins, when one pursues and the other watches.

Paul understood discipline as severe mercy. To the Corinthians, dealing with a man in serious sin, he prescribes a painful step — but his stated goal is "that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 5:5). The severity serves the salvation. And when the discipline has done its work, Paul turns immediately to restoration: "you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow" (2 Corinthians 2:7). The same apostle who prescribed the severity prescribes the restoration. Because the severity was never the point. The restoration was always the point. Discipline that does not aim at restoration is not discipline. It is vengeance with a religious face.

I have failed on the side of avoidance far more than on the side of harshness, and I suspect most pastors of my temperament have. I have watched sheep stray and told myself that pursuing them would be heavy-handed, that grace meant letting them go, that I was being merciful by saying nothing. I was not being merciful. I was being comfortable. I was protecting my own ease and my own reputation as a kind and non-confrontational man, and I was calling my self-protection grace. The straying sheep did not need my comfortable silence. They needed a shepherd willing to walk out into the wilderness and bring them back, at the risk of their anger and the cost of my own peace. I chose my peace. I did this, and the sheep paid for it.

There is a discipline that is abusive, and we must not pretend otherwise. The shepherds of Ezekiel ruled "with force and harshness," and church history is littered with discipline weaponized — the rod turned against the flock, correction used to control rather than to restore, the machinery of accountability captured by men who loved power more than people. This is real, and it is evil, and the abandonment of discipline by many churches is partly a reaction to having seen it abused. But the answer to abused authority is not abandoned authority. It is authority restored to its proper shape and direction — exercised gently, aimed at restoration, carried out by men who would rather suffer than dominate.

The marks of healthy discipline are not hard to name. It is private before it is public, following the escalation Jesus laid out, never beginning with exposure. It is aimed at restoration, not punishment, and it stops the moment the sheep turns home. It is carried out by men who are themselves under discipline, who confess their own sin, who approach the straying brother "in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted" (Galatians 6:1). And it grieves. Discipline that does not grieve has already gone wrong. Paul wrote to the Corinthians "out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:4). The tears are the proof that the discipline is love.

So the under-shepherd is caught between two failures, and most of us only fear one of them. We fear becoming the harsh shepherd, and rightly. But we rarely fear becoming the negligent one, the shepherd who lets the sheep stray because pursuit is costly. Both are failures of love. Both leave the sheep worse off. The harsh shepherd drives the sheep away with the rod; the negligent shepherd lets them wander off the cliff while he watches from the comfort of the meadow. Neither one is the Good Shepherd, who leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one until he finds it.

Go after the one. It will cost you. It is supposed to.
chapters.verdict: A church that will not discipline does not love its people. It only likes them.
reflect: Have you neglected discipline because you mistook avoidance for grace?
Is the goal of your correction always restoration, or sometimes self-protection?
Who has been allowed to harm themselves or the flock because confrontation felt unloving?

chapters.title: Knowing Them by Name
chapters.summary: The Good Shepherd knows His sheep individually, and pastoral care that does not descend to the particular soul is not shepherding but management.
chapters.body:
"He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out" (John 10:3). This single phrase undoes most of what modern ministry has become. The Good Shepherd does not relate to His flock as a crowd. He knows them individually, calls them by name, and the sheep know His voice in return. "I know my own and my own know me" (John 10:14). The relationship is particular, personal, mutual. It is not the relationship of a speaker to an audience. It is the relationship of a shepherd to named, known, individual sheep.

This is the hardest word in the book for the successful pastor, because everything about scale works against it. The bigger the flock grows, the harder it becomes to know the sheep by name, and the stronger the temptation to relate to the congregation as an audience to be addressed rather than a flock to be known. We learn to speak to the room. We learn to handle souls in the aggregate — attendance numbers, giving trends, demographic categories. And the slow tragedy is that a man can pastor thousands while shepherding no one, because shepherding happens one named sheep at a time and addressing a crowd is a different activity entirely.

Richard Baxter saw this clearly, and his *Reformed Pastor* is essentially an extended argument that ministers must know and personally instruct their people one by one. He committed himself and urged his fellow ministers to catechize and counsel every family in the parish individually, household by household, soul by soul. He believed that public preaching, however good, was insufficient without the personal, particular labor of knowing each person and applying the truth to their actual condition. Baxter's vision was relentless and exhausting and impossible to fake, and that was the point. You cannot fake knowing someone by name. You either do the slow particular work or you do not.

The economy of the crowd is seductive because it is efficient. One sermon reaches hundreds. One program serves dozens. The pastor who thinks in crowds can feel enormously productive — look how many he reached, how many attended, how the numbers grew. But the Shepherd of John 10 does not think in crowds. He thinks in names. And the under-shepherd who wants to follow Him has to resist the gravity of scale and keep descending to the particular soul — the actual person with the actual marriage falling apart, the specific doubt, the named grief, the individual sin. This is inefficient. It does not scale. It is also the only thing the Bible calls shepherding.

I feel this tension every week, and I do not always resolve it well. There is a satisfaction in addressing the crowd that the particular work never gives. The sermon that lands with the whole room offers an immediate reward that sitting for two hours with one struggling soul does not. And so the pull is always toward the platform and away from the kitchen table, toward the audience and away from the individual. I have caught myself knowing my congregation's numbers better than their names, tracking the trends while losing the people, relating to the flock as a thing to be grown rather than a set of souls to be known. I have managed when I should have shepherded. I did this.

The names matter to God, and this should reorder our sense of what counts. The genealogies that bore the modern reader are God's insistence that individuals matter, that He keeps track of names. The Good Shepherd "calls his own sheep by name" because names are how persons are distinguished from crowds, and God deals in persons. When Jesus encountered people, He did not process them through a program. He stopped for the one. The woman at the well. The man at the pool. The tax collector in the tree. The Shepherd's pattern is the interruption of the crowd for the sake of the named individual, and the under-shepherd who is always too busy with the crowd to stop for the one has stopped imitating his Master.

There is a humility in this that the platform fights against. Knowing sheep by name requires being among them, low to the ground, present in the unglamorous details of their lives. It requires the pastor to be available to the unimpressive, the difficult, the slow — the sheep who will never improve his numbers or enhance his reputation. The crowd rewards the pastor with applause. The named individual often rewards him with nothing but the knowledge that he was faithful to a soul God loves. And this is precisely the test. The shepherd who only attends to the sheep who reward him is feeding himself again, choosing the sheep who give back the wage of affirmation, and neglecting the weak and the sick exactly as Ezekiel charged.

Peterson made the case, across his whole body of work on pastoral vocation, that the pastor's primary unit is the individual person in the particularity of their actual life, and that the abstraction of ministry into programs and crowds was a loss of the thing itself. He resisted the language of the pastor as a leader of an organization and recovered the older language of the cure of souls — the care, one at a time, of named persons before God. The phrase is worth recovering. The cure of souls. Not the management of an institution. The care of named, individual, particular souls, one slow person at a time.

How does a pastor of a large flock actually do this? Not by personally knowing every sheep — that has limits, and the New Testament's plurality of elders exists partly to extend the knowing beyond what one man can hold. But by refusing the spirit of the crowd. By ensuring that under the structure, every sheep is known by name by someone who is genuinely shepherding them. By the senior shepherd modeling the particular care that the whole flock then learns to give. The goal is not that one man knows everyone. The goal is that no one is unknown, that no sheep is allowed to dissolve into the anonymous mass where the wolves do their best work, because the unknown sheep is the unprotected sheep.

The sheep who is known by name is the sheep who is hard to lose. When the shepherd knows you, your absence is noticed. When the shepherd knows your name, your straying is pursued. When the shepherd knows your story, your sin is confronted in the specific shape it takes in your specific life. The knowing is what makes all the rest of shepherding possible. Without it, there is no pursuit, because you cannot pursue a sheep whose absence you never registered. There is no feeding, because you cannot feed a soul whose hunger you do not know. There is only crowd management, however spiritual its vocabulary.

So learn the names. Slow down for the one. Resist the gravity of the platform that wants to convert your flock into an audience. The Good Shepherd calls His sheep by name, and the under-shepherd who will not do the same has chosen the easier work of speaking to a crowd over the harder work of knowing a soul.

You cannot shepherd a crowd. You never could. There is no such thing.
chapters.verdict: You cannot shepherd a crowd. You can only manage one.
reflect: Do you know your flock as individuals or as an audience?
Whose name and story have you let blur into the mass?
What part of your ministry treats souls in the aggregate rather than one at a time?

chapters.title: The Watch in the Night
chapters.summary: Pastoral accountability is not metaphorical — Scripture says the shepherd will give an account for the souls in his charge, and this reckoning should shape every ordinary decision.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in Hebrews that should never let a pastor sleep too comfortably. "Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account" (Hebrews 13:17). Read it again, slowly, with your own name in the role of the leader. You are keeping watch over souls. And you will have to give an account. The accounting is not a metaphor and it is not optional. It is a fixed appointment, and every soul in your charge will be on the ledger.

This is the doctrine that the comfortable pastorate has quietly buried, because it makes everything heavier. It is more pleasant to think of ministry as a job with reasonable hours and reasonable expectations, a profession one performs adequately and then sets down. But Hebrews will not allow that framing. The shepherd is keeping watch over souls — a night-watchman's image, a man awake while others sleep, scanning the dark for the predators that come when the flock is most vulnerable. And the watch is not for nothing. It is "as those who will have to give an account." The watchman answers to the one who set him over the gate.

James sharpens the same blade. "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness" (James 3:1). Greater strictness. The teacher, the shepherd, the one entrusted with souls, is held to a higher standard precisely because more was entrusted to him. This is the logic of the parable of the talents and the parable of the faithful and wise manager — "everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required" (Luke 12:48). The pastor has been given much. Souls have been placed in his charge. And the requirement scales with the gift.

What does it mean, practically, that I will give an account for the souls in my care? It means that the ordinary decisions of an ordinary week are not as ordinary as they feel. The sheep I neglected this week will be on the ledger. The hard conversation I avoided, the straying member I did not pursue, the sermon I did not labor over because I was tired, the weak one I let fall off the edge of the calendar — these are not merely lapses in productivity. They are failures of a watch I will have to answer for. The reckoning reaches back into the most mundane choices of the most forgettable weeks, and it gives them a weight that the calendar never showed.

I do not live in the light of this as I should. I will confess that plainly. There are weeks I have treated as ordinary that were not ordinary, because every week is a week I will answer for. There are souls I have let blur into the background of a busy season, telling myself I would attend to them later, as though the watch had a pause button. The honest truth is that I often work as a man who will be paid rather than as a man who will answer — attending to what is urgent and visible, neglecting what is eternal and hidden, because the paycheck rewards the visible and the reckoning is far off and easy to forget. The reckoning is not far off. It only feels far off. I have lived as though it were not real. I did this.

The accountability cuts in two directions, and Hebrews captures both. The shepherd keeps watch, and the sheep are told to obey and submit so that the shepherds may "do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you" (Hebrews 13:17). The passage assumes real authority — the sheep are to submit — and it grounds that authority in the shepherd's accountability. The pastor's authority is not arbitrary. It flows from the fact that he will answer for the flock, and a man who will answer for souls must have some real charge over them. This is the connection the egalitarian instinct misses. The authority and the accountability are the same thing seen from two sides. You cannot have one without the other. Strip the authority and you have a shepherd who will be held responsible for sheep he was never permitted to lead. Strip the accountability and you have authority that answers to no one, which is exactly the tyranny we have spent this book warning against.

The night-watch image deserves dwelling on, because it captures the loneliness of the pastoral vocation in a way nothing else does. The shepherd watches while the flock sleeps. The sheep do not see the watch; that is the point of the watch. The congregation rests, untroubled, because someone is awake in the dark scanning for wolves, and most of the flock will never know the nights the shepherd spent watching. There is no applause for the watch. The reward for a night of faithful watching is a flock that wakes safe and never knows it was in danger. The shepherd who needs to be seen will not keep the watch, because the watch is invisible by design. Only the man who is content to be unseen by the flock, because he is seen by the One he answers to, will stay awake when the field is dark and no one is watching him watch.

Bonhoeffer, writing in the shadow of a regime that demanded the church's silence, understood that the cost of keeping watch over souls might be everything. The shepherd who will answer to God rather than to men must sometimes keep a watch that the powers of his age forbid, and he must keep it anyway, because the account he will give is not to the powers but to the Chief Shepherd. This is the seriousness that the doctrine of accountability injects into the vocation. It makes the pastor answerable to a court higher than the congregation, higher than the denomination, higher than the culture. He keeps watch as one who will give an account, and the account is to God.

There is dread in this, and there should be. But Hebrews does not leave the shepherd in dread alone, because the same letter that names the accounting also names the Chief Shepherd as "the great shepherd of the sheep" who was brought back from the dead and who equips His people with everything good to do His will (Hebrews 13:20-21). The One to whom we give account is not a hard master we have never met. He is the great Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep, who keeps watch over the watchmen, who will judge with both perfect justice and perfect mercy. The accounting is real and it is severe, but it is rendered to the One who loves the sheep more than we do and who first kept the watch we are imitating.

So keep the watch as a man who will answer. Let the coming reckoning reach down into the ordinary weeks and make them serious. Pursue the straying one this week, not someday, because someday is not promised and the ledger is being written now. Stay awake in the dark when no one sees, because Someone sees, and He is the One who set you at the gate.

The day of the accounting is coming. It is not a sermon illustration. It is an appointment. And every soul you were given will be there.
chapters.verdict: You will give an account for them. Live as though that day is real, because it is.
reflect: If you gave an account for your flock today, which souls would you struggle to speak of?
Does the coming reckoning shape your ordinary weeks, or only your sermons about it?
Are you keeping watch as one who must answer, or merely working as one who will be paid?

chapters.title: The Plurality and the Solitary Heart
chapters.summary: The New Testament places shepherding in the hands of a plurality of elders, not a solitary leader, and this design protects both the flock and the shepherd from the dangers of the isolated heart.
chapters.body:
The New Testament does not imagine the lone shepherd. We have inherited a model that does — the singular pastor, the visionary leader, the one man whose name is on the church and in whose hands all authority finally rests — but the apostles built something different. They appointed elders, plural, in every church (Acts 14:23). Paul writes to "the overseers and deacons" of Philippi (Philippians 1:1), plural. He instructs Titus to "appoint elders in every town" (Titus 1:5), plural. The shepherding of the flock of God is, in the apostolic design, a shared labor among a plurality of shepherds, and this is not an administrative detail. It is a protection, and the protection runs in both directions.

It protects the flock. A plurality of shepherds means the sheep are not dependent on the gifts, the health, or the integrity of one man. When one shepherd fails — and shepherds fail — the others remain. When one shepherd's blind spot would have led the flock astray, the others can see what he cannot. The flock under a plurality is held by many hands, and many hands are harder to slip through than one. The single-shepherd model, by contrast, places the entire weight of the flock on one man's faithfulness, and when that man falls, the whole flock falls with him. We have watched it happen too many times to pretend the design does not matter.

But it also protects the shepherd, and this is the part the strong leader resists. The man who answers to no other shepherd is a man whose blind spots go unchallenged, whose sins go unconfronted, whose drift toward the hireling goes unnoticed until the wolf reveals it. The plurality of elders is the means by which shepherds shepherd one another — the means by which the watchman is himself watched, the means by which the man who keeps watch over souls has someone keeping watch over his. Without it, the shepherd is alone on the watch, and the lone watchman is the one most likely to fall asleep, or worse, to begin feeding on the flock he was set to guard.

Peter, charging the elders, writes to them as a fellow elder. "I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder" (1 Peter 5:1). The apostle does not stand over the elders as a singular authority. He stands among them as one of them. Even Peter, even an apostle, locates himself within the plurality rather than above it. This is the spirit the design is meant to cultivate — shepherds who see themselves as one among several, accountable to the others, not towering above them as the indispensable one whose judgment may not be questioned.

I have to write this chapter against my own grain, because the solitary heart is mine. There is something in me — and I suspect in most men drawn to lead — that prefers to answer to no one, that experiences genuine accountability as an intrusion, that would rather be the lone shepherd whose vision is unobstructed and whose decisions are unquestioned. I have felt the resistance to plurality rise in my own chest when other elders saw something I did not want seen, when the shared nature of the shepherding got in the way of what I wanted to do alone. That resistance is not strength. It is the hireling's solitude, the isolation in which the shepherd slowly forgets he is accountable and begins to act as though the flock were his. I have felt it. I have indulged it. I did this.

The danger of the isolated heart is not primarily that the lone shepherd will do something dramatically evil. It is subtler and slower than that. The isolated shepherd loses the capacity to see himself. He has no one with the standing and the access to tell him when he is wrong, when his motives have drifted, when the wage has quietly become the reason. We are all of us experts at self-deception, and the shepherd is not exempt — if anything he is more vulnerable, because his role gives his self-deceptions a spiritual vocabulary and a position of authority to defend them. The plurality of elders is God's mercy against this. It places around each shepherd other shepherds who can see what he cannot and who have the standing to say it.

This is why the qualifications for elders in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are mostly about character rather than competence. "Above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1 Timothy 3:2-3). Notice how little of this is about skill. Almost all of it is about the kind of man the elder is when no one is watching. And the reason character dominates the list is that the plurality of elders only works if the elders are the kind of men who will tell each other the truth and receive it. A plurality of cowards is no protection. A plurality of yes-men is no protection. The design requires men of character who will exercise the mutual watch the structure makes possible.

There is a counterfeit plurality that must be named, because it is everywhere. It is the board of elders who exist on paper but never actually challenge the lead pastor — handpicked, dependent on him, lacking the standing or the courage to confront him. This is plurality in name and monarchy in fact, and it provides none of the protection the real thing provides. The lone shepherd with a rubber-stamp board is more dangerous than the honest lone shepherd, because he has the appearance of accountability without the substance, and the appearance lets him and everyone else pretend the protection is in place when it is not. Functional accountability is the question, not formal accountability. Who actually has the standing and the access to tell you the hard truth, and will they actually say it?

Calvin's Geneva built its church government around exactly this conviction — that authority in the church should be plural, exercised by a body of elders rather than concentrated in one man, precisely because concentrated power in the church had proven so dangerous. The Reformed tradition's insistence on plural eldership and connectional accountability was not bureaucratic preference. It was a sober reckoning with what isolated ecclesiastical power had done, and a structural answer to it. The structure cannot make men holy. But it can make their unholiness harder to hide and easier to confront, and that is no small mercy.

This is also why the Pastors Connection Network exists, and why I believe in it past the point of mere strategy. A pastor in an isolated church, with a dependent board and no peers who can see his life, is a shepherd alone on the watch, and the lone watchman is the one the wolf finds. Pastors need other pastors — not for networking, not for resources, though those have their place, but for the mutual watch that the apostolic design assumes and the isolated pastorate destroys. A shepherd needs other shepherds who can see him, who have the standing to tell him the truth, and who will keep watch over his soul as he keeps watch over the flock's.

So submit to the plurality, especially if everything in you resists it. The resistance is the symptom. The shepherd who most wants to be alone on the watch is the shepherd who most needs the others beside him, because the desire for solitude in the office is the early form of the desire to be unaccountable, and the unaccountable shepherd is the one who eventually devours.

Find the men who can see you. Give them the standing to say it. Keep watch over each other in the dark.
chapters.verdict: The shepherd who answers to no one will eventually devour the sheep he answers for.
reflect: Who has the standing to tell you the truth and the access to see when you are wrong?
Are you functionally accountable to other shepherds, or only nominally?
What in you resists genuine plurality, and why?

chapters.title: When the Chief Shepherd Appears
chapters.summary: The whole vocation resolves at the return of the Chief Shepherd, when the under-shepherds will give their account and receive the only reward worth having — and this hope is what sustains faithfulness through an unrewarding ministry.
chapters.body:
Everything in this book bends toward a single horizon, and Peter names it in the same breath as the charge to shepherd. "Shepherd the flock of God that is among you... and when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory" (1 Peter 5:2, 4). The under-shepherd's labor is not open-ended. It runs until an appearing. There is a day coming when the Chief Shepherd returns, when the borrowed staff is handed back, when the account is given and the reward is received. And the whole vocation only makes sense in the light of that day.

The phrase "unfading crown" is set deliberately against the fading kind. Peter knows the under-shepherd is tempted by crowns that fade — the recognition, the platform, the numbers, the name remembered for a generation and then forgotten. These are real rewards and they fade in real time. The faithful shepherd is offered a different crown, one that does not fade, and the choice between the two is the choice that quietly governs every ministry. The man collecting fading crowns will shepherd one way. The man waiting for the unfading crown will shepherd another. And from the outside, for a long time, the two can look identical, right up until the appearing, when it becomes clear which crowns a man was actually working for.

This is the hope that makes an unrewarding ministry sustainable, and most ministry is unrewarding by the world's measure. The faithful pastor of a small church in a forgotten town, feeding a flock that will never make him famous, pursuing the straying sheep no one else would bother with, keeping the watch through nights no one sees — by every visible metric, this man is unrewarded. The fading crowns pass him by. And the doctrine of the Chief Shepherd's appearing is what makes his faithfulness rational rather than foolish. He is not unrewarded. He is waiting for a reward that has not been distributed yet, from a Shepherd who has not yet appeared, and the delay is not denial. The crown is unfading precisely because it is given at the end and lasts forever.

I need this horizon more than I admit, because without it the unrewarding parts of the work make no sense, and most of the work is unrewarding. The faithful sermon that no one praises. The pursuit of the difficult sheep who never thanks you. The watch kept through the dark night that the flock sleeps through and never knows about. If this life is all there is, that labor is foolishness, and the man pouring himself out for sheep that do not reward him is wasting his one existence. But the Chief Shepherd is going to appear. And when He does, the labor that looked wasted will be revealed as the only labor that was ever worth anything. I hold this horizon imperfectly. There are weeks I forget it entirely and work for the fading crowns like everyone else. I did this, and I do this. But the horizon is there whether I remember it or not, and it is coming whether I am ready or not.

The accounting we considered earlier reaches its climax here. The shepherd who keeps watch "as those who will have to give an account" (Hebrews 13:17) gives that account at the appearing. This is where the ledger is read. And the parable of the talents tells us the shape of that moment — the servants who were faithful with what they were given hear the words every shepherd longs for: "Well done, good and faithful servant... enter into the joy of your master" (Matthew 25:21). Not "well done, successful servant." Not "well done, famous servant." Faithful. The Chief Shepherd's commendation is for faithfulness with the flock entrusted, not for the size of the flock or the fame of the shepherd. The man who kept the small flock faithfully and the man who kept the large flock faithfully hear the same words, because the words are about faithfulness, not scale.

What will the under-shepherd hand back at the appearing? This is the question that should haunt and guide every ordinary week. The staff was borrowed; it will be returned. The flock was Christ's; it will be handed back. And the only question is what condition the flock is in when the Chief Shepherd takes it back into His own hands. Did the under-shepherd feed it or consume it? Did he keep the watch or sleep through it? Did he pursue the straying or let them wander? Did he lead the sheep through the valley or abandon them at its edge? The appearing is the moment all of this becomes visible, when the flock is handed back and the Chief Shepherd sees what was done with what He entrusted.

The terror and the comfort of this are the same terror and comfort we met in the first chapter, now arrived at their conclusion. The terror is real: the shepherd will give an account, and the account will be honest, and the fading crowns he collected instead of feeding the sheep will be revealed as the worthless things they always were. But the comfort is greater: the One who appears is the great Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep, the One who already kept the perfect watch, the One whose own faithfulness covers the under-shepherd's failures. The under-shepherd does not stand at the appearing on the basis of his own record. He stands on the basis of the Chief Shepherd's blood, the same blood that bought the flock he was tending. He is, before he is a shepherd, a sheep — kept by the One he served, forgiven by the One he answers to.

Augustine, near the end of his life, was honest about the weight of having borne the office of shepherd, the fear of the account he would render for the souls he had carried. He did not approach the appearing with the confidence of a man certain of his own faithfulness. He approached it as a man who had labored seriously and now cast himself on the mercy of the One he had served. This is the right posture. Not the swagger of the shepherd who thinks his record will carry him. Not the despair of the shepherd who knows it will not. But the sober, hopeful casting of an imperfect under-shepherd on the perfect Chief Shepherd, who is also his Savior.

So the book ends where it must, on the horizon it has been bending toward from the first page. The staff is borrowed, and it will be handed back. The flock is Christ's, and it will be returned to Him. The watch runs until an appearing, and the appearing is coming. Feed the sheep until the Chief Shepherd comes. Keep the watch through the nights no one sees. Pursue the straying one at the cost no one will reward. Lead the flock through the valley and not around it. And when He appears, hand Him back His staff and His flock, and let Him say what He will say.

The man who shepherded for the fading crowns will have collected them, and they will fade in his hands as he watches. The man who shepherded for the One he loved will receive the crown that does not fade, from the Shepherd whose face he has longed to see.

He is coming. The staff is not yours. Feed His sheep until He takes it back.
chapters.verdict: Feed the sheep until the Chief Shepherd comes, and then hand Him back His staff.
reflect: What are you doing now that you would be ashamed to present at His appearing?
Is the unfading crown enough, or are you collecting the fading kind?
When He comes, will you hand Him back a flock you kept, or one you consumed?
